Pipelines & Energy

Keep the line covered, supported and in service.

Creeks, rivers and drainages keep moving after a pipeline goes in. When cover is lost or a bank retreats toward the right-of-way, the line is exposed to loads and forces it was never designed to carry.

What we see in pipelines & energy.

What you're seeingWhat's driving itHow we solve it
What you're seeing

The line is exposed at a crossing.

Cover has washed out and pipe is visible in the bed or banks of a creek or river crossing.

What's driving it

Bed degradation and scour at the crossing, often set off by changes upstream or downstream that lower the channel.

How we solve it

We investigate the crossing and trace the cause, then engineer and permit protection that restores cover and holds the bed in place.

What you're seeing

A free span needs support.

The line spans a gap, by design or because the ground beneath it has washed away, and needs support from below.

What's driving it

An engineered crossing that calls for support, or flow that has removed material beneath the line faster than the channel can rebuild it.

How we solve it

We engineer and install support under the span and, where erosion opened it, stabilize the surrounding site so the gap does not grow.

What you're seeing

The bank is retreating toward the right-of-way.

The outside bend is cutting back, and each high-water event takes more ground toward the line.

What's driving it

High-velocity flow concentrated against the bank as the channel migrates.

How we solve it

We model how the river is behaving and redirect the flow away from the bank, armoring it where the river leaves no room to recover.

What you're seeing

A headcut is moving toward the line.

A step or drop in the channel bed is working its way upstream toward the crossing.

What's driving it

A lowered channel downstream. Every flow event pushes the drop further upstream.

How we solve it

We engineer grade control that stops the headcut where it is and stabilizes the channel through the crossing.

In the field

Meandering creeks see changing water levels and flow rates, and they can expose a pipeline quickly.

Over time, erosion can leave a line spanning a gap it was never meant to cross. That calls for prompt work: support beneath the line and armoring around it.
